claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy contains residual porosity and microcracks.
The starting alloy has a homogeneous FCC matrix.
Residual porosity and microcracks promote preferential nucleation and growth of brittle oxides at high oxygen partial pressure.
Defect-accelerated oxidation initiates crack propagation and can lead to catastrophic failure.
HIP treatment at approximately 800 °C and 150 MPa for 2 hours will reduce porosity and microcrack density.
Reducing defects by HIP will delay or reduce oxidation-driven degradation, especially in oxidizing environments.
Porosity and microcracks act as preferential sites for oxide nucleation and growth.
Oxidation at the defects produces continuous or localized brittle oxide scales.
Residual pores and cracks are high-surface-energy sites that accelerate oxidation under high oxygen partial pressure.
Defect-assisted oxidation forms brittle Cr-rich and Ti-rich oxide phases.
The Cr-rich and Ti-rich oxides compromise the ductile FCC matrix and promote stress concentration and crack propagation during thermal cycling.
Under high-oxygen exposure, HIP-treated samples will have thinner and more discontinuous oxide scales than as-built samples.
Under high-oxygen exposure, HIP-treated samples will show less internal oxidation than as-built samples.
Under high-oxygen exposure, HIP-treated samples will retain higher tensile strength and fracture toughness than as-built samples.
Exposure to inert gas containing 1–2% O2 will cause less aggressive oxidation than exposure to pure O2.
The performance difference between HIP-treated and as-built samples will be smaller in inert gas containing 1–2% O2 than in pure O2.
The proposed governing behavior applies around 800–850 °C for exposure durations up to 100 hours.
The proposed behavior may not apply at substantially lower temperatures or substantially different oxygen potentials because oxidation kinetics change.

contradictions.description: The atmosphere containing inert gas with 1–2% O2 is initially described as a low-oxygen condition but is later called reducing and a baseline of minimal oxidation. An O2-containing atmosphere is oxidizing rather than intrinsically reducing, so the stated gas chemistry and its classification are inconsistent.
